messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: new web site
parts:
We rolled out an update to the Stan web site just now:

http://mc-stan.org/

Hopefully this will make it easier to navigate and
find what you're looking for w.r.t. Stan, RStan,
and PyStan.


New content:

* RStan, PyStan, CmdStan: broken out into own pages

* Team: dev team updated to include Allen Riddell, the developer of PyStan;

* Issues: more info on issue reporting and feature requesting
with issue trackers for Stan, RStan, and PyStan linked

* Source: a page of links to the source repos for RStan, PyStan and CmdStan

* Citations a list of papers that cite and/or use Stan (feel free to contribute
more by posting to this list)

* Index: generalized the description of the page's meta tags for search
snippets


New format:

* consistent nav bar

* logo on header

* everything updated with icons for external links and pdf links

* a new color scheme, arrived at by compromise after a predictably
long discussion (see: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_law_of_triviality)


We're still trying to keep it simple, with links out to RStan and PyStan
and CmdStan Wiki sites rather than a repetion of content on mc-stan.org.


Suggestions or comments always welcome on any aspect of the Stan project.


- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: new web site
parts:
Thanks for the feedback.


HTML vs. PDF:

The only reason we don't convert the manual to HTML is that it's
written in LaTeX and we couldn't get any of the PDF to HTML
converters working robustly. If you can suggest a converter
that produces reasoanble output and doesn't take forever to configure
or use, I'm game to try it.

Writing something like the Stan manual directly in HTML is just
too painful and time-consuming for us.

We used to store the whole API doc online, but that's just
confusing for most users, who have no interest in the C++ code
and documentation.


Searching for "Stan":

The problem with searching for "stan" is that it's a common
name. Let's just say we debated the issue and those in favor
of a simple, high-frequency name won out over those of us who were in
favor of optimizing search engine access. The term "rstan" is much less
frequent, so easier to search for. The mailing list is for
all of Stan, so it's not because there's more mailing list comments
on RStan than Stan.

You can do site-specific searches on the groups from their web pages.
But it's not very good at relevance ranking since there's not much
inter-page link information for Google to exploit.

- Bob

messages.author: b3204700228e4afb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: new web site
parts:
This Wikibook page contains a lot of information for converting latex files to other formats:

http://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/LaTeX/Export_To_Other_Formats#Convert_to_HTML

and I have tried TeX4ht (http://tug.org/applications/tex4ht/mn.html) for various conversions. But all these programs may not be perfect.

I know the manual because quite large now and may not be easily converted to other forms.

Because this is about documentation, I also have a related question about some part and chapter tiles:
"III Programming Techniques": this part contains descriptions about compound data types (Arrays, vectors...) and statistical modeling with Stan language. Data types information may be more suitably put in IV which also contains some contents for data types. I think this part III can be more beautifully named Statistical modeling with Stan language or similar names. You may call IV as "Stan language Reference". The order of these two can be reversed also.  

There should also be a small section to explain how users can set up their own direction some where in their hard drive to compile a stan program (xxx.stan).

Thanks for your great work!

Z. Su

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: new web site
parts:
On 12/6/13, 4:03 PM, Z. Su wrote:
> This Wikibook page contains a lot of information for converting latex files to other formats:
>
> http://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/LaTeX/Export_To_Other_Formats#Convert_to_HTML
>
> and I have tried TeX4ht (http://tug.org/applications/tex4ht/mn.html) for various conversions. But all these programs may
> not be perfect.

The install instructions look rather daunting:

http://tug.org/applications/tex4ht/mn-unix.html

And the first instruction they give fizzles out at:

http://tug.org/applications/tex4ht/mn.html

indicating the author died and new development's not going forward.

Our main problem is that we just don't have time to do all
of these things given our gazillion-item-long to-do list.
We also don't want to tie our releases or web site to a single
developer's personal machine, so we'd need to get these things installed
on our integration server.
> I know the manual because quite large now and may not be easily converted to other forms.

Size shouldn't matter --- it's a program after all.
In my experience, it's a matter of these programs not handling
user-defined macros, LaTeX sources in different files, etc.

> Because this is about documentation, I also have a related question about some part and chapter tiles:
> "III Programming Techniques": this part contains descriptions about compound data types (Arrays, vectors...) and
> statistical modeling with Stan language.

My intention was to have the programming techniques be about
how to use Stan and the language reference be the definitive guide
to what it's supposed to do, but not about how to use it.

Having said that, we do plan to reorganize the manual soon to allow
us to describe the samplers more cleanly. And that's going to
require a new part of the manual.

> Data types information may be more suitably put in IV which also contains some
> contents for data types. I think this part III can be more beautifully named Statistical modeling with Stan language or
> similar names. You may call IV as "Stan language Reference". The order of these two can be reversed also.

We wanted to put the programming first and reference manual after,
figuring most users wouldn't want to dive into the reference manual.

We could've put them in separate docs following the way R has
a whole bunch of manuals, but we decided it'd be easier to just
have one. At some point it might get so huge we'll have to change
gears. We may or may not strip out the command-line instructions
in the future the same way that PyStan and RStan have their own
manuals.

> There should also be a small section to explain how users can set up their own direction some where in their hard drive
> to compile a stan program (xxx.stan).

Not sure what you're asking for in this last paragraph.

- Bob

Thanks for the link. It looked promising in terms of installers
and easy-to-understand doc. But it crapped out on our title
page:

$ pandoc -s stan-reference.tex -o stan-reference.text

stan-reference.text
pandoc:
Error at "source" (line 153, column 14):
unexpected "*"
expecting letter or new-line
\date{\vspace*{36pt} \Stan Version

I tried a simple standalone example with a * command inside a macro
call and it doesn't work. This is not giving me confidence in its
ability to parse LaTeX input files and I don't have time to fiddle our
manual into something parseable by pandoc.

If someone else wants to take on translating our manuals from
LaTeX to HTML, we'd be happy to host them. I don't have the
inclination (or even the time) to learn pandoc's markdown and
write out manuals in that format.

- Bob

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: new web site
parts:
I played around using pandoc to convert LaTeX -> HTML.  The only things giving it problems were the use of \vspace in the \date macro and the use of the \Verb macro (which it didn't recognized as starting a verbatim area). Editing those out produced a reasonable result, although it didn't translate all the macros; what I noticed was that \sf, font sizes, and the custom macros like \fitem, \farg didn't translate.  The branch https://github.com/jrnold/stan/tree/feature/pandoc-manual has the results of my hacking.

If you want to support LaTeX->PDF & HTML output, then my best guess is that the easiest way to do that would be to rewrite the reference in pandoc's markdown and then use pandoc to convert it into LaTeX to PDF and HTML, using specialized templates and snippets of LaTeX or css for each conversion. It may still work with the original in LaTeX if the problem LaTeX is removed, but might require a little heavier postprocessing to get HTML output.
I'm not saying its worth the time to do that, but as far as I am aware, that would be the easiest way to do.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: new web site
parts:
The nice thing about pandoc is that it has really good support for BibTeX references (http://johnmacfarlane.net/pandoc/README.html#citations).  Using the options specified in http://johnmacfarlane.net/pandoc/README.html#citation-rendering, I could get the HTML output to have references (although it loses the linking and backreferences in the LaTeX version).

I was able to get the conversion to have a table of contents with internal links to the sections, and footnotes work. The pandoc reader converts the macros like \refsection to something like Section [referencename], but the HTML output doesn't link them. There has to be a way to do this, I just haven't figured it out yet.
